summary: Specifies a way to describe typed relationships between web resources, called link relation types, and sets up a registry for them. It also defines the HTTP Link header field for carrying such links. It was a standards-track specification and was replaced by RFC 8288.

plainLanguage.summary: A web page often needs to say what one resource is to another: that one is the next chapter, or the licence that applies. This RFC defines a common way to say that, a list of standard relationship names, and the HTTP header used to carry them.

subtitle: Typed links between web resources, a registry of link relation types, and the HTTP Link header.

tldr.problem: HTML and Atom could each describe a relationship between two resources, but they did it in separate, incompatible ways, and a resource with several representations could not state its relationships once and reuse them everywhere.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a link as a context IRI, a relation type, a target IRI and optional target attributes. Relation types are either registered names from an IANA registry or extension URIs, and the Link HTTP header is defined as one serialisation of the model.
tldr.outcome: RFC 5988 was a standards-track specification. It has been obsoleted by RFC 8288.

facts.label: Registered relation name syntax
facts.value: Starts with a letter, then letters, digits, dot or hyphen

sections.title: Why Typed Links Need a Common Format
sections.content:
A means of indicating the relationships between resources on the Web, as well as indicating the type of those relationships, has been available for some time in HTML and more recently in Atom. These mechanisms, although conceptually similar, are separately specified. Links between resources need not be format specific, and it can be useful to have typed links that are independent of their serialisation, especially when a resource has representations in multiple formats.

This document defines a framework for typed links that is not specific to a particular serialisation or application. It does so by redefining the link relation registry established by Atom to have a broader domain, and adding to it the relations that are defined by HTML.

An HTTP header field for conveying typed links had already been defined, in Section 19.6.2.4 of RFC 2068, but was removed from RFC 2616 because of a lack of implementation experience. Since then it has been implemented in some User Agents, for example for stylesheets, and several additional use cases have surfaced.

Because the header had been removed, the status of the Link header was unclear, which led some to consider minting new application-specific HTTP headers instead of reusing it. This document addresses that by re-specifying the Link header as one such serialisation, with updated but backwards-compatible syntax.
sections.plainLanguage: Two formats were doing the same job separately, and an HTTP header for the job had been tried and then withdrawn. This RFC brings them into one shared scheme and puts the header back in use.

sections.title: What a Link Is
sections.content:
In this specification, a link is a typed connection between two resources that are identified by Internationalised Resource Identifiers. A link is comprised of a context IRI, a link relation type, a target IRI, and optionally target attributes.

A link can be viewed as a statement of the form "{context IRI} has a {relation type} resource at {target IRI}, which has {target attributes}".

Two practical notes follow. In the common case the context IRI will also be a URI, because many protocols such as HTTP do not support dereferencing IRIs. Likewise the target IRI will be converted to a URI in serialisations that do not support IRIs, such as the Link header.

The specification places no restrictions on the cardinality of links: there can be multiple links to and from a particular IRI, and multiple links of different types between two given IRIs. Likewise the relative ordering of links in any particular serialisation, or between serialisations such as the Link header and in-content links, is not specified and is not significant in this specification. Applications that wish to consider ordering significant can do so.

Target attributes are a set of key and value pairs that describe the link or its target, for example a media type hint. This specification does not attempt to coordinate their names or use, but it does provide common target attributes for use in the Link HTTP header. The specification defines no general syntax for expressing links and mandates no specific context for any given link; serialisations of links are expected to specify both aspects.
sections.plainLanguage: Every link says three things: what it is about, what kind of relationship it is, and where it points. It can carry extra notes, such as the language of the target.

sections.title: Link Relation Types
sections.content:
In the simplest case, a link relation type identifies the semantics of a link. A link with the relation type "copyright" indicates that the resource identified by the target IRI is a statement of the copyright terms applying to the current context IRI. Relation types can also indicate that the target resource has particular attributes or exhibits particular behaviours; a "service" link, for example, implies that the identified resource is part of a defined protocol, in that case a service description.

Relation types are not to be confused with media types. They do not identify the format of the representation that results when the link is dereferenced; they only describe how the current context is related to another resource. Relation types should not infer any additional semantics based upon the presence or absence of another link relation type, or on their own cardinality of occurrence, with one exception: the combination of the "alternate" and "stylesheet" registered relation types has special meaning in HTML4 for historical reasons.

There are two kinds of relation type. A registered relation type is a well-defined type registered as a token for convenience and to promote reuse by other applications. Registered names must conform to the reg-rel-type rule and must be compared character by character in a case-insensitive fashion. They should be appropriate to the specificity of the relation type, so that more general names stay available for less specific use. Registered relation types must not constrain the media type of the context IRI, and must not constrain the available representation media types of the target IRI, but they can specify the behaviours and properties of the target resource, such as the allowable HTTP methods or the request and response media types that must be supported.

An extension relation type is used by applications that do not wish to register a relation type. It is a URI that uniquely identifies the relation type. Although the URI can point to a resource containing a definition of the semantics, clients should not automatically access that resource, to avoid overburdening its server. Extension relation types must be compared as strings, after converting to URIs if serialised in a different format such as a Curie, in a case-insensitive fashion, character by character. Because of this, all-lowercase URIs should be used for extension relations.
sections.plainLanguage: A relation type has two jobs: name the kind of connection, and say what it means. Some names are registered for everyone to use; anything else is identified by a URI the application invents.

sections.title: The Link Header Field
sections.content:
The Link entity-header field provides a means for serialising one or more links in HTTP headers. It is semantically equivalent to the LINK element in HTML and to the atom:link feed-level element in Atom.

The grammar is a link-value in angle brackets followed by any number of semicolon-separated link parameters. The parameters include rel for the relation type, anchor to override the context, rev, hreflang, media, title, title* and type, plus an extension mechanism.

Each link-value conveys one target IRI as a URI-Reference inside angle brackets. If the URI-Reference is relative, parsers must resolve it as per RFC 3986, and any base IRI from the message's content is not applied. By default the context of a link conveyed in the Link header field is the IRI of the requested resource. The anchor parameter overrides this with another URI, such as a fragment of this resource or a third resource. Consuming implementations can choose to ignore links with an anchor parameter, in which case the entire link is to be ignored, and they must not process the link without applying the anchor. Depending on the HTTP status code and response headers, the context IRI might be anonymous, with no context IRI available, as on a 404 response to a GET request.

The rel parameter must not appear more than once in a given link-value; occurrences after the first must be ignored by parsers. The rev parameter has been used in the past to indicate that the semantics of the relationship are in the reverse direction: a link from A to B with REL="X" expresses the same relationship as a link from B to A with REV="X". It is deprecated by this specification because it often confuses authors and readers, and in most cases using a separate relation type is preferable. Extension relation types are required to be absolute URIs in Link headers, and must be quoted if they contain a semicolon or a comma.

The target attributes are hreflang, media, title, title*, type and any link-extension parameters. The hreflang parameter is a hint indicating what the language of the result of dereferencing the link should be, and it is only a hint: it does not override the Content-Language header of the response obtained by following the link. Multiple hreflang parameters indicate that multiple languages are available from the indicated resource. The media parameter indicates the intended destination medium, and there must not be more than one in a link-value. The title parameter labels the destination so that it can be used as a human-readable identifier, and the title* parameter encodes that label in a different character set and can carry language information. If both appear, processors should use the title* value. The type parameter is a hint about the media type of the result of dereferencing the link, and there must not be more than one in a link-value.
sections.plainLanguage: The header writes the target in angle brackets and then lists its properties after semicolons. Which resource the link is about defaults to the page being fetched, unless an anchor parameter says otherwise.

sections.title: The Registries
sections.content:
Three registries are set up. The Link HTTP header registration updates the Message Header registry entry for "Link" in HTTP to refer to this document; the header field is Link, the applicable protocol is http, its status is standard, and the change controller is the IETF.

The Link Relation Type registry is established by this specification, which also updates Atom to refer to it in place of its own Registry of Link Relations. Relation types are registered on the advice of a Designated Expert appointed by the IESG or their delegate, with a Specification Required. A registration request consists of a template giving the Relation Name, a Description, a Reference, optional Notes and optional Application Data, and is sent to the link-relations mailing list. Within at most 14 days the Designated Expert will either approve or deny the request, communicating the decision to the review list and IANA. Denials should include an explanation and, where applicable, suggestions for how to make the request successful. Decisions, or the lack of them, can be appealed first to the Application Area Directors and then to the full IESG. IANA should only accept registry updates from the Designated Expert.

The Link Relation Application Data registry allows entries in the relation type registry to be extended with application-specific data, and is registered the same way, with its own template giving the Application Name, a Description, a Default Value and optional Notes.
sections.plainLanguage: New relation names go through a named expert, who has two weeks to approve or reject them, and an approval can be appealed.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The content of the Link header field is not secure, private or integrity-guaranteed, and due caution should be exercised when using it. The use of Transport Layer Security with HTTP is currently the only end-to-end way to provide such protection.

Applications that take advantage of typed links should consider the attack vectors opened by automatically following, trusting, or otherwise using links gathered from HTTP headers. In particular, Link headers that use the anchor parameter to associate a link's context with another resource should be treated with due caution. The Link entity-header field makes extensive use of IRIs and URIs, and the security considerations for those apply.
sections.plainLanguage: Anyone who can change the header can change what the client believes about the page, so the header needs the same protection as the page itself.

data.title: The syntax of one Link header field
data.code:
Link       = "Link" ":" #link-value
link-value = "<" URI-Reference ">" *( ";" link-param )
link-param = ( ( "rel" "=" relation-types )
           | ( "anchor" "=" <"> URI-Reference <"> )
           | ( "rev" "=" relation-types )
           | ( "hreflang" "=" Language-Tag )
           | ( "media" "=" ( MediaDesc | ( <"> MediaDesc <"> ) ) )
           | ( "title" "=" quoted-string )
           | ( "title*" "=" ext-value )
           | ( "type" "=" ( media-type | quoted-mt ) )
           | ( link-extension ) )

viz.caption: A SELECTION OF REGISTERED LINK RELATION TYPES (RFC 5988)

items.label: Next
items.desc: Refers to the next resource in an ordered series of resources.

items.label: Prev
items.desc: Refers to the previous resource in an ordered series of resources. Synonym for 'previous'.

items.label: Alternate
items.desc: Designates a substitute for the link's context.

items.label: Describedby
items.desc: Refers to a resource providing information about the link's context.

items.label: License
items.desc: Refers to a license associated with the link's context.

items.label: Self
items.desc: Conveys an identifier for the link's context.

items.label: Stylesheet
items.desc: Refers to an external style sheet.

items.label: Via
items.desc: Identifies a resource that is the source of the information in the link's context.
